Royal Bank of Canada stock gains appeal from cash-back overhaul
sum: Royal Bank of Canada announced enhanced rewards for two cash-back credit cards on Monday, November 2, 2026. The changes affect the RBC Cash Back Mastercard and the RBC Cash Back Preferred World Elite Mastercard, with new earning structures already in effect and more flexible redemptions planned for December.

FT.com reported that RBC added uncapped cash-back earning rates across everyday spending categories. The standard RBC Cash Back Mastercard now offers 2% on groceries, 1% on gas, electric-vehicle charging, rideshare and transit, and 0.5% on other net purchases.

The Preferred World Elite card offers 3% on groceries, dining, gas, electric-vehicle charging, transit, rideshare, streaming and digital gaming. Other net purchases earn 1%. The card also adds out-of-province and out-of-country emergency medical coverage, flight-delay and delayed-baggage insurance, and mobile-device insurance.

RBC said the new earning structures took effect automatically for existing and new cardholders on October 1, 2026. The standard card retains its zero-dollar annual fee. The Preferred World Elite card carries a $120 annual fee for the primary cardholder and $50 for each additional cardholder.

Starting December 2, cardholders will be able to redeem cash back at any time through RBC Online Banking or the RBC Mobile app once their balance reaches $1. RBC said balances can be checked through either channel and rewards will accumulate indefinitely. The announcement also gives cardholders more control over when they claim rewards instead of relying on a scheduled payout.

For investors, the announcement expands RBC's consumer-card proposition rather than changing the bank's earnings outlook. The immediate focus is execution: the new rates must support customer engagement while the lower redemption threshold and digital access simplify the reward process.
Royal Bank of Canada stock traded at 182.21 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 14:08 CET on Wednesday, November 11, 2026.

TD vs. Royal Bank: Which Dividend Stock Would I Buy With $10,000?
sum: Choosing a bank for your next $10,000 can feel like choosing between two familiar branches on the same street. The businesses differ once you follow the earnings. One offers a recovery opportunity with more repair work. The other offers a broader earnings mix at a price that already reflects much of its strength. I’d let that tradeoff decide the purchase before a small yield difference gets too much attention.

Toronto-Dominion Bank (TSX: TD) combines a major Canadian retail franchise with substantial U.S. operations and wholesale banking. Its domestic customer base gives it a strong foundation. The U.S. business adds opportunity, alongside the compliance work and operating constraints that have shaped its recent strategy. I’d view the stock as an established bank working through a specific recovery, with a demanding route back to stronger growth.

Third-quarter adjusted earnings reached $2.77 per share, up 26% year over year. That’s encouraging evidence that the recovery is reaching each share. Its common equity tier 1 ratio was 14.3%, providing a substantial capital buffer. Together, the figures support the case that TD can continue rewarding shareholders while funding the work needed to improve the business.

The $1.12 quarterly dividend, or $4.48 annualized, uses about 40% of the latest adjusted quarterly earnings. The catch is execution in the United States. Regulatory constraints and compliance costs can keep the bank from using all its strengths as freely as investors would like, which is the price of owning the recovery opportunity.

Royal Bank of Canada (TSX: RY) adds substantial wealth management, commercial banking, insurance, and capital-markets operations to its retail banking base. That gives it more ways to earn than Canadian mortgage and deposit growth alone. I’d favour that mix for an investor wanting a bank they can hold through changing conditions without depending on one turnaround programme delivering exactly on schedule.

Its third-quarter adjusted earnings were $4.28 per share, up 11%, with a common equity tier 1 ratio of 13.5%. The quarterly dividend is $1.76, consuming about 41% of that adjusted earnings figure. Both banks therefore have meaningful room behind their latest payments, even though the growth rates and capital ratios differ.

RBC Launches Auto-Callable Enhanced Return Barrier Notes Linked to Five Major U.S. Bank Stocks, Maturing 2029
sum: On November 4, 2026, Royal Bank of Canada filed a free writing prospectus outlining the terms for Auto-Callable Enhanced Return Barrier Notes tied to a basket of five prominent U.S. financial-sector equities, with maturity set for November 29, 2029.
- Issuer and CUSIP: The Notes are issued by Royal Bank of Canada (CUSIP 78018DRB5), traded on NYSE under the ticker RY.

- Basket Composition: The basket includes five equally weighted stocks: Bank of America (BAC), Citigroup (C), Goldman Sachs (GS), Morgan Stanley (MS), and Wells Fargo (WFC), each representing 20% of the basket.

- Auto-Call Feature: If on November 30, 2027, the basket’s closing value is at or above the Initial Basket Value of 100, the Notes will be automatically called, with investors receiving a minimum of $1,132.50 per $1,000 principal, equating to at least 113.25% of principal.

- Enhanced Return at Maturity: Should the Notes not be called and the Final Basket Value exceed the Initial Basket Value, investors will earn a return equal to 150% of the Basket Return, as detailed in the filing.

- Barrier Level: The Barrier Value is set at 70, which is 70% of the Initial Basket Value; if the Final Basket Value falls below this threshold, investors will incur a loss of 1% of principal for every 1% decline below the Initial Basket Value.
- Initial Estimated Value: The filing estimates the initial value to range between $902.50 and $952.50 per $1,000 principal, which is below the public offering price.

items.t: The Bank of Canada Is Worried About Inflation: These 2 Stocks Might Not Be
sum: On October 28, 2026, the Bank of Canada raised its policy rate by 0.25%, marking the first hike since July 2023. The central bank held the benchmark steady at 2.25% for seven consecutive meetings before sounding the alarm. Inflation spiked to 3.1% in September 2026, sending policymakers on high alert.

During the post-meeting press conference on Wednesday, Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem explained the monetary policy decision. He cited the Middle East oil shock and unresolved Canada-US trade relations as major reasons for the upward rate adjustment to 2.5%. Macklem is increasingly worried about inflation risks.

In response, TSX declined modestly by 0.04% the day after and remains up 14.3% year-to-date. However, if more rate hikes are on the horizon, investor sentiment could shift. They could rotate from rate-sensitive sectors and speculative growth stocks into lower-risk investments. Energy, for one, continues to benefit directly from surging oil prices. Banks could see higher margins on loans and mortgages.

Royal Bank of Canada (TSX: RY) will hold up regardless of the economic environment. The $396.5 billion bank is the largest TSX company by market capitalization. Its scale and diversified business model provide peace of mind, not to mention the 156-year dividend track record.

President and CEO David McKay said Royal Bank of Canada continues to raise the bar globally to deliver exceptional, record results. In Q3 fiscal 2026, net income rose 11% to a record $6 billion versus Q3 fiscal 2025. For the nine months ended July 31, 2026, provision for credit losses (PCL) fell 10.5% year-over-year to $3 billion.

RY trades at $288.21 per share (+26.4% year-to-date) and pays a 2.5% dividend. Look beyond the price, as you’d be investing in a bedrock of stability and an anchor stock. The banking giant increased its prime rate by 25 basis points to 4.7% effective October 29, 2026. It will expand its net interest margin capacity

Canadian Natural Resources (TSX: CNQ) is a solid choice for long-term dividend income and capital growth. Notably, Macklem said rising inflation is energy-driven. This large-cap energy major boasts long-life, low-decline oil sands assets, allowing for consistent production increases. It also operates on exceptionally low break-even costs.
